candidates.title: Munbyn’s adorable AI printer turns your kid’s weirdest ideas into quirky stickers
candidates.full_text:
Back in 1998, Nintendo sold a tiny thermal printer that hooked up to your Game Boy and printed grainy Game Boy Camera photos onto sticker paper. It was gloriously pointless, and I wanted one more than I wanted world peace. Those pixelated stickers ended up on lunchboxes, diaries, and the occasional bedroom wall, much to parents’ dismay. Nearly three decades later, the idea is back as a holiday gift built to get kids creating instead of scrolling. MUNBYN’s SP01 is a thermal sticker printer for kids, and where Nintendo’s needed a camera, this one runs on imagination and a microphone.

Kids press and hold a chunky red button on top, describe whatever they’re dreaming up, and AI turns it into black-and-white line art. That drawing prints on BPA-free thermal sticker paper, ready to be colored in, stuck down, and traded. MUNBYN mostly makes shipping-label printers, so the inkless hardware is familiar territory, but the bright yellow, toy-box styling is a fun new look for the brand. The mic only listens while the button is held down, which should put parents at ease. It costs $99.99 (available at a discounted $55.99 right now), and the AI side doesn’t come with a monthly bill.

Click Here to Buy Now: $55.99 $99.99 ($44 off). Hurry, deal ends in 48-hours! Amazon Link Here.

The SP01’s chunky yellow shell looks like a TV set from a Saturday morning cartoon, with rounded corners, an embossed MUNBYN wordmark on top, and a little smiley face molded into the side. The star of the show is that oversized red button, borrowed straight from the vocabulary of game-show buzzers and arcade cabinets. Hold it, talk, let go, and the printer comprehends your prompt back out loud with a little jingle before it prints. The 3.5-inch screen sits tilted back 10 degrees, which MUNBYN says is meant to help with posture and eye comfort. The one-press lid is designed to be child-friendly and to protect children’s soft fingernails. With a gentle press, the lid pops open easily, so kids can change the paper themselves without needing an adult’s help or having to pry the lid open. Also, no scissors are needed to tear the stickers. Kids can simply follow the visual guide on the top of the machine and tear the paper accordingly, which allows them to get a clean, neat edge without using scissors.

The button also doubles as the privacy policy, and I think it’s the smartest call on the whole device. The microphone only listens while it’s held down, so there’s no always-on assistant eavesdropping on dinner, and MUNBYN says voice data is processed on the device itself. MUNBYN also skipped the sharp cutter blade found on most label printers, so kids pinch, pull, and peel stickers off the roll. You’ll want scissors handy for neat edges, a fair trade for keeping blades away from seven-year-olds. Best of all, that screen shows sticker previews and menus, with no feed, no autoplay, and nothing to scroll.

Every sticker prints as black-and-white line art at 203 DPI, on BPA-free thermal paper that needs no ink, toner, or cartridges. The printhead moves at roughly 2 inches (50mm) per second, so the wait between saying “a pig wizard” and holding an actual pig wizard is short enough to keep a kid’s attention. The color happens afterward, with markers, crayons, and whatever else is rattling around the craft drawer. Out of the box you get three sticker rolls and a blank sketchbook to stick finished creations into, which is basically a starter scrapbook. A Photobooth mode turns four quick photos into a printed strip, mall photo booth style, minus the mall.

That monochrome output makes the AI a starting point and leaves the finishing to the kid. Coloring books have worked this way for well over a century, handing you outlines and trusting you with everything inside them. Stickers add the bit that made the 90s sticker binder so addictive, which is that you can trade them, gift them, and slap them on a sibling’s homework. A sticker a kid dreamed up, printed, and colored becomes something they actually made, and that feeling beats any number of likes. Digital art apps can do plenty, but none of them let you peel the result off and put it on a water bottle.

The SP01 lists at $99.99 and is currently $55.99 on MUNBYN’s US store as part of an early Black Friday deal, and it’s on Amazon too. candidates.title: This tiny aluminum carabiner flips into a table hook with one simple twist
candidates.full_text:
The carabiner has had a wild career. It started as the Karabinerhaken, German for “carbine hook,” a clip that let soldiers attach their carbines to a belt. Climbers adopted it in the early 1900s, and somewhere along the way it ended up holding the keys of every college student, dad, and barista on the planet. Now KOLABO, a travel accessories brand out of Los Angeles, has taught it a new trick. The Axl HOOK is a carabiner with an arm that rotates out into a hook, so you can hang your bag off a table instead of dumping it on the floor.

Designed with Copenhagen studio Wahl&Ross, the Axl HOOK takes the shape of a soft-cornered triangle. One corner hides a pivot, and the integrated rotating mechanism allows the hooked arm to swing outward . A rubber tip at the end is designed to grip the table surface so your bag stays put. The whole thing is forged and CNC-machined from 6061 aluminum, measures 2.76 x 2 inches (70 x 51 mm), and weighs a feathery 1.1 ounces (32 grams). KOLABO rates it for 48 pounds (22 kg), offers it in Matte Black or Matte Silver, and lists the retail price at $28. First soldiers, then climbers, and now commuters who just want somewhere to put their tote bag.

Click Here to Buy Now: $22 $28 (21% off). Hurry, only 411/500 left!

The entire transformation hinges (literally) on one integrated pivot tucked into a corner of the triangle. A single screw anchors the joint, and the hooked arm rotates around it, swinging up and away from the body until it stands proud of the frame. Fold it back and the arm nests into the triangle’s outline, so the carabiner looks like a plain carabiner again with nothing poking out. KOLABO sums up the motion as press, rotate, hook, and that really is the whole user manual. I’m a big fan of mechanisms you can figure out without squinting at an instruction card, especially ones you’ll be working one-handed with a coffee in the other.

A discreet rubber pad caps the end of the arm, adding grip right where metal meets tabletop. That little tip is meant to keep the hook from skating across glossy café counters or lacquered wood when a heavy bag starts tugging on it. On the opposite side, a solid spring-loaded gate handles regular carabiner duty, snapping shut when you let go. It’s a straight, chunky bar instead of a skinny wire, which suits the object’s sculpted look and gives your thumb a broad surface to press. Clip it to a belt loop, a water bottle, or a bag strap between stops.

KOLABO builds the Axl HOOK from 6061 aluminum, an alloy containing magnesium and silicon that shows up everywhere from bike frames to camera rigs. The parts are forged first and CNC-machined second. Forging presses the metal into shape under enormous force, aligning its grain structure for toughness, while machining carves in the crisp edges and precise detailing. KOLABO lists a maximum recommended load of 48 pounds (22 kg), enough for a packed laptop bag, a grocery tote, or a weekender stuffed with questionable souvenirs. It’s built for bags and keys rather than people, so keep it far away from your climbing harness.

The frame measures 2.76 x 2 x 0.39 inches (70 x 51 x 10 mm), small enough to disappear into a palm. At 1.1 ounces (32 grams), your keyring will barely register the extra passenger. The 10mm thickness keeps the profile slim against a bag strap or inside a pocket. Every edge is rounded and the tube-like arms carry soft, continuous curves, intended to keep them from snagging fabric or digging into your hand. Matte Black leans architectural and minimal, while Matte Silver reads clean and technical. Personally, I’d go black for how it turns the triangle into something close to jewelry.

Axl HOOK came out of a collaboration between KOLABO in Los Angeles and Wahl&Ross in Copenhagen, with final refinements worked out alongside a precision manufacturing partner in Taiwan. The development photos show walls of sketches and rows of 3D-printed prototypes in different shapes and proportions. The Copenhagen link is laser-engraved right into the frame, along with the studio’s coordinates, a sweet little postmark of where the design took shape. Even the box gets a minimal printed carton with a line drawing of the hook that you’ll probably keep in a drawer for no reason. Axl HOOK is the first product from KOLABO, a Los Angeles-based design brand focused on rethinking everyday travel essentials.
